name: Grafana
tagline: Open-source analytics and monitoring platform for metrics visualization.
description: Grafana draws dashboards from pluggable data sources and layers alerting on top of the same queries that feed those panels.
pros: Metrics, logs, and traces held in separate stores can be drawn on one dashboard without first being copied into a single database.
The self-hosted build carries no license fee, and this repository's pricing analysis records no built-in caps on users or retention for it.
Grafana Cloud's free tier is documented here with metrics series, log volume, and retention allowances plus pre-built dashboards for common stacks.
Alert rules attach to the query that renders a panel, so a threshold and its chart cannot end up describing different things.
Dashboards built on Prometheus carry forward when logs and traces are added to the same view later.
cons: Running the open-source build yourself moves cost into operations: servers, database management, backups, and upgrades all land on the team.
Grafana displays telemetry rather than producing it, so Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, or equivalent collectors have to run alongside it.
A data source without a maintained plug-in becomes a development project before its numbers can appear on any panel.

content.title: What Grafana is
content.body: Grafana is a visualization and alerting layer for telemetry that already lives somewhere else: metrics stores, log systems, trace backends, and other sources are reached through plug-ins and drawn as panels on dashboards. This repository files it under Developer Tools at 4.5/5 from 2,260 reviews and ranks it second on its monitoring tools page, behind Datadog. The audience recorded for it runs from small teams to enterprise, and because the open-source base is free, the entry cost is engineering time rather than a license.

content.title: Panels, dashboards, and the query behind each one
content.body: A Grafana dashboard is a grid of panels, and each panel is bound to a query against a single data source. Layout, time range, and template variables are set at the dashboard level, which is how one screen can put request latency from a metrics store beside error text from a log store beside spans from a trace store. The data stays where it already lives and the dashboard is simply the place it meets. The consequence runs the other way too: panel quality depends entirely on the queries written behind each panel.

content.title: Data sources and the plug-in model
content.body: Grafana does not own a data store for your telemetry; it reaches out to sources you already run, and the plug-in model is how new ones are added. That positioning explains the rest of this page, because dashboards, panels, and alert rules are all downstream of a connection that already works. The connections recorded across this repository, spanning the products whose reviews happen to mention Grafana, look like this:
items: Prometheus: the open-source write-up here describes Grafana as the visualization half of a Grafana-Prometheus monitoring stack.
Logs and traces: the same article has Grafana rendering Prometheus data alongside logs, with Loki and Tempo named as companion stores elsewhere in this repository.
Kubernetes: the Kubernetes review lists Grafana among its monitoring integrations.
Docker: the Docker review records Grafana used for container dashboard visualizations.
GitLab: the GitLab review records Grafana dashboards embedded inside GitLab for performance monitoring.
Anything else: a source without a bundled connector is added through the plug-in model rather than rejected by a fixed list.

content.title: Alerting written from panel queries
content.body: Grafana's alerting runs on the expressions that draw the panels. A threshold set on a query therefore describes exactly what the chart shows, and alert configuration cannot drift away from its dashboard through a second, parallel definition maintained somewhere else. This is also how the product earns a monitoring role rather than a reporting one: rules evaluate on a schedule and notify through configured channels, so the same dashboard a person reads during the day is the definition that produces the notification at night.

content.title: Self-hosted build or Grafana Cloud
content.body: Two deployment shapes sit under one name. The open-source build runs on infrastructure the team manages; this repository's monitoring pricing analysis records it as free with no built-in user or retention caps, and lists server capacity, database management, backups, and upgrade work as costs the license price does not cover. Grafana Cloud is the managed alternative, offered in tiers with increasing retention, user limits, and support, and its free tier is recorded in the stack guide here with specific metrics, log, and retention allowances. The dataset stores a list price band of $29-200/mo for the paid side.

content.title: Limits that follow from the plug-in shape
content.body: Because Grafana displays rather than collects, an organization needs telemetry pipelines in place before dashboards mean anything, and those pipelines need owners of their own. Plug-in coverage then decides what can be charted: an unmanaged source becomes custom development rather than a checkbox. A self-hosted install converts a license line into operational work, since upgrades, database care, and backups fall to whoever runs it. None of these read as defects; they are the shape of a tool positioned between your data and the people reading it.

content.title: Grafana next to Datadog, New Relic, and the open-source stack
content.body: The head-to-head records stored with this review place Grafana at 4.5/5 above New Relic at 4.2, CircleCI at 4.3, and JFrog at 4.1, and below Datadog at 4.6, Docker at 4.6, GitHub at 4.7, and Postman at 4.6 — the last three being neighbors rather than substitutes. Datadog and New Relic sell collection together with the interface. The best-of-breed note in this repository instead pairs Grafana with Loki for logs and Tempo for tracing, aimed at teams willing to do the configuring. That difference, not the rating, is the real fork.

content.title: Basis of these notes
content.body: These judgments come from the vendor's published material and from this repository's stored comparisons, monitoring pricing analysis, and category notes; no Grafana instance was operated to write them. What the evidence supports is a specific reader: a team holding several telemetry backends that wants one place to draw and alert on them, with either the appetite to self-host or a managed tier to pay for. Our dataset holds 4.5/5 from 2,260 reviews, and records no compliance certifications for the product.

faqs.question: Is Grafana free to run on our own hardware?
faqs.answer: The open-source build is free to self-host. The pricing analysis in this repository notes the tradeoff: servers, database management, backups, and upgrades become costs the license price does not cover.

faqs.question: What does Grafana Cloud include at no cost?
faqs.answer: The stack guide here records a free tier with 10,000 metrics series, 50 GB of logs, 14-day retention, and pre-built dashboards for Node.js, Postgres, and Next.js stacks.

faqs.question: Does Grafana collect metrics itself?
faqs.answer: No. Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, or other collectors feed it. The open-source write-up in this repository describes Grafana as the visualization layer of that stack rather than the collection layer.

faqs.question: How does Grafana compare with New Relic in this dataset?
faqs.answer: Grafana holds 4.5/5 against New Relic's 4.2 in the stored comparison records, and the two use different billing shapes: a $29-200/mo band here against New Relic's per-user and ingestion model.

faqs.question: Can a dashboard query raise an alert?
faqs.answer: Yes. Alert rules are written against the same query that draws the panel, which is how Grafana's role extends past displaying charts into notifying on them.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Dashboards come quickly; alert routing, plug-in configuration, and query work take substantially longer
whoShouldUse: Organizations holding several telemetry backends — Prometheus, logs, traces — that want one place to draw dashboards and define alerts, with the option to self-host.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams with no telemetry pipelines in place yet, or those that want collection and interface from one vendor instead of a visualization layer over stores they run.
